title: Curse the day (Job 3)
hook: Job curses the day he was born, and the Bible keeps every word

segments.voice: Yesterday, three friends sat with Job seven days and seven nights, the custom later called shiva. Your line was they said nothing. Today, the silence breaks, and Job is the one who breaks it.

Seven days of quiet, and then: "After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day." Two chapters ago, this same man said the LORD gave and the LORD hath taken away, blessed be the name of the LORD. The adversary bet he would curse. Now the first thing out of his mouth is a curse. But the text is precise about the target. Not God. His day, the day he was born. Everything he's held since the messengers came is about to pour out.
screen: `AFTER THIS OPENED JOB HIS MOUTH.` → `HE CURSED HIS DAY.` → `NOT GOD. HIS DAY.`

segments.voice: He begins: "Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived." Erase it from the calendar. "Let that day be darkness; let not God regard it from above, neither let the light shine upon it." Then he goes further, and it's hard to hear: "Why died I not from the womb?" If he'd never lived, he says, he'd be lying still, in the place where the small and the great are together, where the prisoners rest. "There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest." This isn't a man being polite to heaven. It's a cry, the whole chapter of it, and it ends with no answer and no resolution. Notice: this is scripture. The Tanakh didn't cut it, soften it, or add a note telling Job to calm down. His rage sits inside the holy books, read and studied word for word. The Writings also hold Lamentations, and psalms that ask God how long. A tradition that keeps words like these is saying something about what may be said, out loud, in front of God. That doesn't make Job right about everything; the friends will argue with him, and so will God. But the book lets him say it first. If your own grief has ever come out angry, you're in the company of a man the book itself called perfect and upright.
screen: `LET THE DAY PERISH.` · `WHY DIED I NOT FROM THE WOMB?` · `THE WEARY BE AT REST.` · `SCRIPTURE KEEPS EVERY WORD.`

segments.voice: Is there something you're angry about that you've kept polite, a diagnosis, an injustice, a person, a year that went wrong? Say it to yourself in plain words, no softening, not to act on it or to judge the feeling, only to let it be said, the way Job said his. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is, rough edges and all.
His day. Not God: the day he was born is the target of Job's curse, the one thing he wants erased. Today's word.
Your line: rage is allowed. Saying it isn't the same as acting on it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition has a long practice of lament: the book of Job, Lamentations read on Tisha b'Av, and psalms that question God are all part of the Tanakh and are read and studied aloud.
